AI Hub: Artificial intelligence for psychometricians

Source: vignettes/articles/ai-hub.Rmd
ai-hub.Rmd

Artificial intelligence (AI) now writes test items, scores essays, predicts item difficulty and drafts analysis code. If you were trained in item response theory (IRT), classical test theory and validity theory, you already have the tools to judge these systems. What is usually missing is the vocabulary, a sense of how the methods work, and practice checking them.

The AI Hub is for that reader: A psychometrician, graduate student or testing-program analyst who knows IRT and some R, but has not trained a machine learning model or called a large language model (LLM). Every topic starts from a job you already do and puts the AI method beside the classical one.

What changes and what does not

AI changes how some parts of a test are produced: Items can be drafted in minutes, constructed responses can be scored as they arrive, and item properties can be estimated before a field test. It does not change what a test has to show. The scores still need evidence that they mean what we say they mean, for the people we use them with. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing apply to an AI-scored test just as they apply to any other.

That is why every AI feature in mirtverse sits behind a psychometric check: Generated items are verified and calibrated, machine scores must agree with human scores overall and within groups, and anything uncertain goes back to a person.

A learning path

Work through the steps in order, or jump to the job you face now. Each step names the question it answers, what to read and what to try in R.

Step The question Read Try in R
1. Vocabulary What do machine learning words mean in measurement terms? Translation table; the AI section of the glossary —
2. ML through an IRT lens How do prediction models differ from measurement models? Book: Machine learning through an IRT lens —
3. LLMs in your workflow How do I use a language model safely for analysis and writing? Scripts from plain language; book: Large language models as a colleague mv_ask(), mv_llm_replay(); simulate_llm_respondents() (experimental)
4. Automated scoring Can a machine score constructed responses as well as raters? Book: Automated scoring; reading list: Automated scoring train_scorer(), agreement_report(), score_open(); Lab 7
5. Item text and difficulty What does the wording of an item tell us before anyone answers it? Book: What item text tells us; reading list: Item text item_features(), predict_difficulty(); Lab 8
6. Automatic item generation How do I generate items and know which ones to keep? Book: Generating items; assessment pipeline; reading list: AIG item_model(), generate_isomorphs(), calibrate_families(), generate_items(), verify_items(); Lab 9
7. Validity and fairness What evidence does an AI component need before it is used? Book: Validity, fairness and governance of AI; reading list: Validity ai_audit(), validity_argument(), dif(); Lab 10

What you can do with AI in mirtverse today

These functions use a language model through the ellmer package. Set one up once with mv_ask_setup(): Claude or OpenAI with your own API key, or a local model through Ollama if your data must stay on your computer.

To try them with no key and no internet connection, turn on replay mode first. Every request is then answered from a file of recorded responses, so the same call always gives the same answer:

library(mirtverse)
mv_llm_replay()      # answer from the example recordings
mv_llm_recordings()  # which requests they cover

The example recordings answer the calls in system.file("replay", "examples.R", package = "mirtverse"), which include the language-model examples below. Their responses were written by hand to show what a model returns, with a few deliberate mistakes for mirtverse’s checks to catch. To capture your own session with a live model and replay it in class, use mv_llm_record().

Write analysis code from a plain-language request 

mv_ask("Fit a graded response model to these attitude items, check the fit and explain the results.",
       data = Science, ask = FALSE)

mv_ask() turns the request into a plan, fills tested code templates and shows you the script before anything runs. Without a provider it falls back to an offline keyword parser. The guide explains what is sent to the model and how to keep column names private.

Generate and verify items 

p <- mv_pipeline("Grade 6 numeracy")
p <- set_blueprint(p, blueprint)     # content areas x cognitive levels
p <- generate_items(p, n = 40)       # drafts with keys and rationales
p <- verify_items(p)                 # a second model answers each item blind
flags(p)                             # wrong keys, weak distractors, duplicates

A second, independent model call answers each multiple-choice item without seeing the key; disagreements are flagged before any person reviews the items. review_packet(p, ai_screen = TRUE) then prepares the human review.

Predict item difficulty from the text 

feats <- item_features(itemtext)          # length, readability, numbers, options, near-duplicates
items <- merge(itemtext, feats)
m <- predict_difficulty(items, c("family", "sentences", "decimals", "max_digits"),
                        se = "b_se")      # LLTM, lasso and random forest, cross-validated
m
tidy(m)                                   # what each feature adds to difficulty
predict_difficulty(items, c("family", "sentences", "decimals"),
                   group = "family")      # hold out whole item families

The LLTM’s weights say what makes items harder; the lasso and the random forest show how much more a flexible model can predict. predict_difficulty() warns when a feature looks like it was computed from the field test itself, and group checks whether predictions hold for a new kind of item rather than a new item of a known kind.

Generate items from item models, and calibrate their families 

area <- item_model(
  stem = "A rectangle is {l} cm long and {w} cm wide. What is its area?",
  key = "{l * w} square cm",
  distractors = c(perimeter = "{2 * (l + w)} square cm", added = "{l + w} square cm",
                  half = "{l * w / 2} square cm"),
  values = list(l = 4:12, w = 2:8), constraints = c("l > w", "(l * w) %% 2 == 0"),
  name = "ARE")
area                                       # how many items it can make, and how many are flawed
items <- generate_isomorphs(area, n = 10)  # isomorphs, with the values they came from
# after the field test, with b and its standard error for each item:
calibrate_families(calibrated, family = "model", se = "b_se")

An item model generates items whose every option comes from a template, so an error in the model can be caught for all its items at once. calibrate_families() then checks after the field test whether the isomorphs are equally difficult, and how large a field test the family mean can replace for a new item.

Audit an AI component, and draft the validity argument 

audit <- ai_audit(aiscored_cr, human2 = "human2", group = "group",
                  item = "item", period = "year")   # agreement, fairness, drift
audit                                               # block / review / info flags
autoplot(audit)
va <- validity_argument(audit, construct = "Grade 8 science",
                        use = "school accountability")
va                                                  # claims, threats, evidence by inference
mv_report(fit, extra = list("Validity argument" = va))

ai_audit() checks a scoring engine against human scores overall, within groups at the same human score, and across administrations or engine versions; with responses it adds DIF on the test as scored, and with components it checks difficulty models and item families too. validity_argument() maps the results to the inferences of a validity argument and lists the evidence still owed, such as human oversight and appeals.

Simulate respondents (experimental) 

items <- itemtext[endsWith(itemtext$id, "-01"), ]
syn <- simulate_llm_respondents(items, personas)   # one request per described respondent
compare_synthetic(syn, setNames(items$p_field, items$id))

simulate_llm_respondents() asks a language model to answer items as described test takers would, and compare_synthetic() checks the answers against real data. Both are experimental: Simulated respondents tend to find items too easy, to answer alike when they are described alike and to play stereotypes, so they can help find unclear items but cannot replace a field test. The book’s chapter on large language models runs the example from the recordings, with the twelve personas in examples.R.

Score open-ended responses, and check the scores 

q <- score_open(q, responses, scorer = "llm")   # or a trained model
q$agreement                                     # machine-human agreement
flags(q)                                        # agreement and fairness gates

The full example in examples.R scores 40 answers from the essays data against a four-point rubric.

To train your own engine instead of calling a language model, use train_scorer(). It learns from human-scored answers, runs offline, and works with score_open() like any other trained model:

e1 <- essays[essays$prompt == "E1", ]
engine <- train_scorer(e1[1:300, ])                 # words and phrases -> human score
test <- e1[301:400, ]
agreement_report(predict(engine, test), test$human1, test$human2,
                 group = test$group)                # QWK, SMD and PRMSE by group

Machine scores pass the same gates whether they come from a language model or from a model you trained yourself: Quadratic weighted kappa against human scores, standardized mean differences overall and within groups, and low-confidence responses routed back to human raters.

How the AI Hub teaches

  • Familiar job first. Each topic opens with a task you already do and shows the AI method next to the classical one, on the same data.
  • Evidence before adoption. Every AI output passes a psychometric check before it counts.
  • Offline by default. Labs and book examples run without an API key or an internet connection, using recorded model outputs (mv_llm_replay()), so a classroom never depends on a provider being up. Live models are an optional extra.
  • Known answers. As in the teaching labs, the AI datasets are simulated with planted problems, and lab_truth() reveals them. itemtext has 192 numeracy items from 12 item families with field-test difficulties; essays has 1,600 short science explanations scored by raters, written so that fluent writers’ answers are longer at the same score; aigfield is a field test of 60 items generated from six item models; aiscored is a test whose written answers an engine scored for two years.

For instructors

Lab 6, on scoring open-ended responses, compares an automated engine with human raters and fits well at the end of an IRT course. Lab 7 goes further: Students train their own engine, judge it on new students, find why it underscores English language learners, and decide how much of the scoring it should do. In Lab 8 they predict item difficulty from the text of 192 numeracy items, find miskeyed items and near-duplicates, catch a leaky feature, and decide how far predictions can replace a field test. Lab 9 builds an item factory: Students fix an item model, calibrate a field test of generated items, find the two families that are not isomorphic and why, and decide when a family mean can stand in for a field test. In Lab 10 they audit an AI-scored test before its scores are released, and turn the audit into a validity argument for a technical advisory committee. The online book has a part on AI in measurement whose chapters work offline, so they can be assigned as readings. The course map puts the chapters and labs together as a four-week module or a one-day workshop, and the workshop kit has slides and a facilitator’s guide for the day. To teach the same topics on your own items or your own engine’s scores, the instructor toolkit builds labs with AI sections on your data, and the teaching assistant can build them for you.
